opus-5.5.text:
Well, with fixed code you at least have a stationary target. You can write a formal specification, you can run a prover, and if you're very careful and the system isn't too large, you can get some confidence that this particular artifact does what you claim it does. Even that is extremely hard in practice. We don't really verify large software today; we verify small components, and we still find bugs in the verifiers themselves.

Now take a system that can rewrite itself. Whatever you proved yesterday was about a different program. So you need to verify not just the current state but every possible future state reachable through self-modification, and that space is essentially unbounded. You're no longer proving "this code is safe." You're trying to prove "this code will only ever turn itself into code that is also safe, forever, under all inputs and environments." That's a fundamentally different and much stronger claim.

There's also the problem that the system may become more capable than the verifier. If it's improving, at some point its modifications are things we can't understand, can't anticipate, and maybe can't even represent in our specification language. You'd want the system to verify its own successor, but now you have an infinite regress. Who verifies the verifier? Each step introduces some probability of error, and over many iterations, even a tiny error rate compounds toward near certainty of failure.

And then there are the classic limits from computability theory. Rice's theorem tells us that non-trivial semantic properties of arbitrary programs are undecidable in general. With fixed code, we cheat by restricting ourselves to nice, constrained programs. A self-modifying superintelligent system is precisely the kind of thing that doesn't stay in the nice, constrained box.

So my view is that with fixed code, verification is hard. With self-improving systems, I think it's not just harder. It may be impossible in principle to get the kind of guarantees we would need. At best you get probabilistic confidence, and probabilistic confidence is not good enough when one mistake could be the last one.

r001.rationale: It explains that verification must ensure every future self-modified state remains safe, identifying preservation of system properties across code changes as the core difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
So, with fixed code, verification is at least a well-defined problem. You have a static artifact, you have a specification, and you can ask: does this artifact satisfy this specification? It's hard, it's expensive, it's often incomplete in practice, but in principle the object you are verifying doesn't change under you. You prove something once, and the proof stays true for as long as the code stays the same.

With a self-modifying system, the thing you verified at time zero is not the thing that exists at time one. The system rewrites itself, or retrains itself, or changes its own goals or its own verification procedure. So any proof you had is about an ancestor of the current system, not the current system. You would need to verify not just the initial state, but every possible successor state, and every successor of those successors, essentially an infinite tree of future versions. And the system is the one generating those versions, so you don't even get to choose which branches to look at.

People sometimes say, well, just verify the modification process. Verify that each self-modification preserves the properties you care about. But that just pushes the problem one level up. Now you need a proof that the verifier itself is correct, and if the system can modify the verifier, you are back where you started. You get a regress. And there are actually formal results that cut against you here, limitations on a system being able to prove things about its own successors, related to Gödel and Löb. A system cannot in general trust its own future reasoning in a way that is fully rigorous.

And there's a practical layer on top of the theoretical one. Even if a modification is tiny, a small change in a very large system can have arbitrarily large consequences. There is no guarantee that small edits produce small behavioral changes, so you can't rely on continuity. You would have to re-verify from scratch after every change, and if the system is changing faster than humans can verify, which is the whole point of a superintelligent self-improving system, you simply lose. Verification time grows, system change rate grows faster.

So my claim is not just that it's harder in degree. It's harder in kind. I think for sufficiently capable, sufficiently self-modifying systems, you end up with something that is in principle unverifiable. You can test it, you can monitor it, you can get probabilistic confidence, but the kind of guarantee people mean when they say "verified safe" is not available. And that matters because the stakes are not like a buggy app. If you're wrong once, you may not get another attempt.

r001.rationale: It explains that each self-modification must be shown to preserve the properties of interest, while changes can have unpredictable effects and prior proofs no longer apply.

astra-6.text:
With fixed code, you have a stable object to analyze. You can ask, “Does this program satisfy these properties under these assumptions?” That’s already difficult, and there are general limits to what you can prove about arbitrary programs.

With a self-modifying system, the object you verified can change. A proof about today’s version doesn’t automatically apply to tomorrow’s version. You now need to establish that every permitted modification preserves the properties you care about—including modifications to the mechanism that evaluates future modifications.

You can constrain the system, require proofs before accepting changes, or keep a verifier outside its control. Those are useful approaches. But then your guarantee depends on those constraints holding and on your formal definition of safety actually capturing what we want in the real world. So the challenge goes from verifying one program to verifying a potentially open-ended sequence of programs and the process that produces them.

r001.rationale: It says verification must establish that every permitted modification preserves the properties of concern, since a proof about one version does not automatically apply to later versions.

sol-6.1.text:
With fixed code, at least you have a stable object you’re trying to verify. You specify the properties you want, and you try to prove that this particular program satisfies them under certain assumptions. That’s already very difficult.

With a self-modifying system, the thing you verified can change. A proof about version one doesn’t automatically tell you anything about version two. So now you need to prove that every modification preserves the properties you care about, including the ability to make safe modifications in the future.

You might say, “Well, require it to produce a proof before accepting each change.” But then you have to trust the proof checker, the specification, and the mechanism enforcing that requirement. Can those be modified? And does your specification actually capture what you mean by safety?

Self-modification isn’t automatically impossible to verify. You can constrain it. But verifying an unrestricted system that can rewrite its own reasoning and verification machinery is a much stronger problem than proving something about one fixed piece of code.

r001.rationale: The response identifies proving that every modification preserves the properties that matter as the central difficulty.
